\section{Generalization and Robustness}
\label{sec:generalization}

Having established depth signal characteristics within individual model--strategy cells (\S\ref{sec:atlas}), we now test whether these signals survive three progressively harder transfer settings: classifier choice (\S\ref{sec:gen:baselines}), cross-model (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossmodel}), and cross-strategy (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}) leave-one-out evaluation.
We close with a negative result on end-to-end learning (\S\ref{sec:gen:e2e}).

\subsection{Baseline Comparison}
\label{sec:gen:baselines}

Table~\ref{tab:baselines} compares six feature-based classifiers and two external anchors on the Pythia nucleus cell (5K samples per depth, d0--d3).
Random Forest (RF), CORAL \cite{cao2020_coral}, and DivEye (gradient-boosted trees) achieve statistically indistinguishable 4-class accuracy: 78.2\%, 78.1\%, and 78.2\%, respectively (pairwise bootstrap $p > 0.05$, Bonferroni-corrected).
Cross-entropy MLP (74.9\%) and logistic regression (75.0\%) trail by 3--4 percentage points, while single-feature perplexity regression (25.1\%) performs at chance.

The parity among RF, CORAL, and DivEye---spanning random forests, rank-consistent ordinal regression, and gradient-boosted trees---demonstrates that discriminative power resides in the 19-dimensional feature set $\mathbf{f}(x)$ (\S\ref{sec:method:features}), not in classifier architecture.
We adopt RF as the default for subsequent experiments owing to its simplicity and scale-invariance (see \S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}).

As an external anchor, DeepSeek V3.2 in a zero-shot prompting setup achieves 40.0\% on 200 Pythia nucleus samples---above chance (25\%) but far below the weakest feature-based method, confirming that depth estimation from raw text is nontrivial even for frontier LLMs.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Baseline comparison on Pythia nucleus (d0--d3, 5K/class). RF, CORAL, and DivEye are statistically indistinguishable ($p > 0.05$, bootstrap with Bonferroni correction). All feature-based methods use the same 19 statistical features.}
\label{tab:baselines}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
Method & 4-Class Acc (\%) & d1v2 AUC \\
\midrule
Random Forest & 78.2 & 0.86 \\
CORAL & 78.1 & 0.82 \\
DivEye (XGBoost) & 78.2 & 0.87 \\
CE-MLP & 74.9 & --- \\
Logistic Regression & 75.0 & --- \\
\midrule
DeepSeek V3.2 (zero-shot) & 40.0 & --- \\
PPL regression (single feat.) & 25.1 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:gen:crossmodel}

We evaluate cross-model generalization via leave-one-out (LOO): train RF on all three strategies of two model families, test on the held-out third.
Mean 4-class accuracy is 66.4\%, well above the 45\% gate and 25\% chance level (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).

\paragraph{Per-class recall reveals structural asymmetry.}
The headline accuracy is inflated by near-perfect d0 recall ($\geq$98.5\% across all holdouts), as the human-written vs.\ machine-generated boundary transfers trivially.
Within generated text (d1--d3), the picture is less favorable: 3-class mean accuracy drops to 55.4\%, and d2 recall is consistently the lowest class.
The Pythia holdout is hardest, with d2 recall of only 26.8\%; OLMo and GPT-2~XL holdouts reach 43.3\% and 52.6\%, respectively.
Figure~\ref{fig:confusion_matrix} visualizes the confusion structure: d2 errors split between d1 and d3, consistent with ordinal confusion where the middle class absorbs prediction mass from its neighbors.

This per-class decomposition reframes the cross-model story.
Depth signal \emph{does} transfer across model families---all holdouts far exceed chance---but the transfer is concentrated at the human/machine boundary (d0 vs.\ d1+), with diminishing fidelity at finer ordinal distinctions.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-model LOO (RF, 4-class). Per-class recall exposes d2 as the consistent bottleneck; near-perfect d0 recall inflates headline accuracy.}
\label{tab:cross_model}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}
\toprule
Holdout & Acc (\%) & \multicolumn{4}{c}{Per-Class Recall (\%)} \\
\cmidrule(l){3-6}
 & & d0 & d1 & d2 & d3 \\
\midrule
Pythia & 62.4 & 100.0 & 49.3 & 26.8 & 73.6 \\
OLMo & 69.2 & 99.3 & 75.5 & 43.3 & 58.8 \\
GPT-2 XL & 67.6 & 98.5 & 74.7 & 52.6 & 44.5 \\
\midrule
Mean & 66.4 & 99.3 & 66.5 & 40.9 & 59.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Cross-Strategy Transfer}
\label{sec:gen:crossstrategy}

The cross-strategy LOO evaluates whether features learned from two decoding strategies generalize to a held-out third, within a single model family.
Mean 4-class accuracy across all nine holdout cells is 59.1\%, again far above chance but substantially below in-distribution performance (Table~\ref{tab:cross_strategy}).

\paragraph{Strategy-dependent transfer hierarchy.}
Nucleus holdouts transfer best (59.9--69.4\%), reflecting nucleus sampling's intermediate entropy profile.
Top-$k$ holdouts are consistently hardest (51.5--54.9\%), likely because truncation at a fixed vocabulary size induces a sharply different distributional signature from the probability-based or temperature-based alternatives.

\paragraph{Temperature-induced d1/d2 inversion.}
When temperature ($\tau{=}0.9$) is held out, d1v2 AUC collapses to 0.13 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.25 (OLMo), indicating that the classifier trained on nucleus and top-$k$ data \emph{reverses} its depth-1 vs.\ depth-2 ordering for temperature-sampled text.
The mechanism is uniform logit scaling: temperature $\tau{<}1$ multiplicatively concentrates the logit distribution at each generation step, accelerating convergence toward the model's attractor distribution.
Consequently, temperature-sampled depth-$N$ text exhibits statistical fingerprints resembling depth-$(N{+}1)$ text under nucleus or top-$k$ sampling, producing systematic depth overestimation.

\paragraph{Z-score normalization: a falsified hypothesis.}
A natural conjecture is that the temperature inversion is a scale artifact correctable by per-feature z-score normalization.
We test this with logistic regression (LR), which unlike RF is scale-sensitive.
Z-score normalization rescues LR overall cross-strategy accuracy (25\%$\to$61\%), confirming that raw LR failure is dominated by feature scale mismatch.
However, z-score normalization \emph{fails} to recover the critical d1v2 pairwise AUC on temperature holdouts: GPT-2~XL drops from 0.50$\to$0.24, and OLMo from 0.50$\to$0.19 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_strategy}).
RF, being scale-invariant by construction, is unaffected by z-score normalization ($\Delta < 0.02$~pp).
The temperature shift is therefore a genuine structural distributional shift, not a correctable scale artifact.
We discuss deployment implications of this finding in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-strategy LOO (RF, 4-class). The d1v2 AUC inversion under temperature holdout persists after z-score normalization of LR features, confirming a structural distributional shift.}
\label{tab:cross_strategy}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
Model & Holdout Strategy & Acc (\%) & d1v2 AUC \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Pythia} & nucleus & 69.4 & 0.69 \\
 & temp ($\tau{=}0.9$) & 62.8 & 0.58 \\
 & top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) & 51.5 & 0.64 \\
\addlinespace
\multirow{3}{*}{GPT-2 XL} & nucleus & 59.9 & 0.78 \\
 & temp ($\tau{=}0.9$) & 56.1 & \textbf{0.13} \\
 & top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) & 53.6 & 0.83 \\
\addlinespace
\multirow{3}{*}{OLMo} & nucleus & 65.4 & 0.79 \\
 & temp ($\tau{=}0.9$) & 58.2 & \textbf{0.25} \\
 & top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) & 54.9 & 0.85 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{@{}l}{\textit{Z-score LR (temp holdout only):}} \\
GPT-2 XL & temp ($\tau{=}0.9$) & 56.4 & 0.24 \\
OLMo & temp ($\tau{=}0.9$) & 55.5 & 0.19 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{End-to-End Learning: A Negative Result}
\label{sec:gen:e2e}

Can a pretrained language model learn depth estimation directly from raw text, bypassing hand-crafted features?
We evaluate two complementary approaches: end-to-end finetuning and contrastive ordinal learning.

\paragraph{End-to-end finetuning.}
We finetune DeBERTa-v3-base \cite{he2021_deberta_v3} and RoBERTa-base \cite{liu2019_roberta} on the Pythia nucleus cell (5K samples/class, 5-fold CV, 3 epochs, lr $2{\times}10^{-5}$).
DeBERTa achieves $58.3\% \pm 4.7\%$ and RoBERTa $59.5\% \pm 3.2\%$---both far below RF at 78.2\% (gaps of $-19.9$ and $-18.7$~pp).
The near-identical performance across two architectures with different pretraining objectives (masked LM vs.\ disentangled attention) establishes this as an architecture-independent finding.

Feature overlap analysis reveals \emph{why}.
Probing DeBERTa's \texttt{[CLS]} representations for our 19 features yields Spearman $\rho = -0.484$ ($p = 0.036$) between feature importance rankings of DeBERTa and RF, with zero overlap among each method's top-5 features.
PLMs excel at encoding surface-level properties (TTR: $R^2 = 0.85$; rep\_2gram: $R^2 = 0.82$), but the perplexity tail statistics that RF relies on---\textsc{var\_surprisal} and \textsc{p90\_ppl}---show negative $R^2$ in DeBERTa representations, indicating that these distributional signatures are not learnable from raw text by standard finetuning.

\paragraph{Contrastive ordinal learning (DCOL).}
We train a contrastive ordinal loss over RoBERTa-large embeddings (LoRA $r{=}16$), designed to enforce ordinal margin structure in the embedding space.
After six iterations (v1--v6) spanning two backbone architectures, the best stable configuration (RoBERTa-large, v6) achieves only 64.5\%---still 13.7~pp below RF---with severe overfitting (train 75\% vs.\ val 64.4\% at epoch~1, early stopping at epoch~4).
Earlier iterations with DeBERTa (v1--v5) uniformly failed due to embedding collapse, OOM, catastrophic forgetting, or NaN gradients.

\paragraph{Synthesis.}
Both approaches converge on the same conclusion: hand-crafted statistical features capture recursive depth signals that PLMs cannot extract from raw text.
The depth signal resides in the tail behavior of the reference-model perplexity distribution---a second-order, cross-model property inaccessible to standard text encoders operating on surface token sequences.
